pets.description: Teddy - 6 months & 20lbs (as of 09/10), Terrier/Shepherd Mix, Neutered We're not sure of this guys breed mix, he's a smaller guy with big do features, a stunner! If you want to see a video of this dog please click here . Expected to be about 35lbs full grown This puppy is eligible to join our foster-to-adopt program. Please email fostertoadopt@socialteesnyc.org with the animal’s name in the subject line if you are interested! Want to straight up adopt? Submit an adoption application a t socialteesnyc.org Their Foster Family Says: " Teddy is SO curious! Listens to the wind. Wants to say hi to other dogs (all sizes) and approaches with energy and playful vibes but then retreats in self consciousness and hides behind my legs. He wants to pick up every stick and leaf and parade them around as his new treasures but drops them easily and moves on to the next street-delight. Teddy has learned “sit” and sometimes gets “paw”! He is treat motivated and highly focused on his bones/chew treats for hours. He also LOVES his human (immediately started to treat me like a mama). He wants to unravel his bones while sitting next to me and when I’m standing up and walking about he will follow me around squeaking and chewing his toy. His noises are soooo sweet. Squeaks and whimpers to express delight and rarely barks — only when someone in the hall of my apartment building startles him. He got something sticky stuck to his tail and I was worried that pulling it off he would be upset but no! He was a patient patient; displaying bravery/kindness even as his tail was jostled and pulled. He's a boy with a sweet and gentle soul and would do best with people who are patient as he continues to figure out how to be brave and make friends." Level of dog ownership experience required: INTERMEDIATE – As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day. The adopter must have relevant primary care experience with a similar breed, temperament, and/or energy level. (Primary care experience includes ownership, fostering, or dog sitting as an adult, not a dog you grew up with.) Relevant puppy care experience is a huge plus, but bare minimum the adopter must have TONS of time and patience. Raising a puppy can be a lot of fun, but it’s also tremendous work. Puppies’ personalities and exercise/stimulation requirements change dramatically between now and when they’re a year old as their bodies and brains develop, so an active lifestyle and the ability to adapt to a pup’s evolving needs are a must. We strongly urge professional dog training with a rewards based trainer from the get go. Adults only or kids ages 8 and up – all puppies go through a mouthy, rambunctious phase and often accidentally hurt children when playing. PLEASE DO YOUR OWN BREED RESEARCH to make sure you have a better understanding of the kind of temperament and exercise requirements this dog may have as an adult. Energy Level: MEDIUM – Very young puppies sleep and nap a lot, but their energy level skyrockets when they become teens (4 months to around a year). As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 60 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day at a minimum. (This is regardless of dog size – many small breeds were designed for lots of activity and will exhibit unwanted behavior when they’re understimulated.) TOLERANCE TO CITY Adjusting to the city – Spooked easily by loud noises and bustling areas but walks pretty well in quiet areas and probably just needs more time to adjust (may be a puppy or a brand new rescue). Would prefer a home in a calmer part of the city or the suburbs. Teddy is easily spooked by loud cars/trucks/sirens. He can be a little skittish at a passing skateboarder. Ideal home would be somewhere calm Although, I think he needs more time to get acclimated. POTTY TRAINING Yes – Few or no accidents. He still relies on wee pads for peeing, as he drinks quite a bit of water. He has learned to go number 2 outside. COMFORT LEVEL WITH STRANGERS Wallflower – Very shy with new people and takes a while to warm up. Afraid when unfamiliar people try to say hi on the street, hides or shrinks back when new people visit the home. Teddy is very timid around strangers. He recoils if a stranger tries to approach him. If a stranger comes to my home, he will bark, but will not approach the person. BEHAVIOR WITH CHILDREN (always requires adult supervision) Maybe for age 12 and up – Is either big and energetic (okay with kids big enough not to get knocked down) or a little skittish (could be comfortable with older children that can be extra gentle) He has moments when he can be mouthy and gets the zoomies. He can be skittish among young children. SOCIAL BEHAVIOR WITH OTHER DOGS Still working on it – Either retreats from other dogs or barks at them/leash reactive. Needs more socialization training or may just be a dog that prefers human company. He is very afraid of dogs larger than him. He shows some interest in smaller dogs, but needs to be trained to approach them calmly. MOUTHY BEHAVIOR Needs training – Is either still in the puppy stage or was never trained. Tries to put their mouth on your hands when playing or needs attention, grabs leash, chews on your personal belongings. Teddy has a propensity to bite hands. I've noticed this occurs after he's energized from a walk. Firm correction usually stops him. He also likes to bite the leash on walks. If left unsupervised, he will try to eat shoes, grabs clothes within reach, eat cardboard, dig in bathroom trashcan. SEPARATION ANXIETY (Please leave your foster dog home alone every day for at least 20 minutes.) Adjusting – Might cry for a few minutes when you first leave the house but settles pretty quickly and has no problem being left alone otherwise. I've left him alone for a couple of hours in some cases, and he does whimper, but the eventually settles down with his chew toys. He's always placed in the crate when I leave him alone, so there's no destruction. As he's a puppy, I cannot trust him to roam around my apt alone. LEASH MANNERS Getting the hang of it – Probably hasn’t been on a leash much in their life but figuring it out. Might be a mild puller but responds to correction. He's still getting the hang of walking on one's side. He tends to zigzag left to right during walks. He sometimes gets eager and starts pulling ahead. He will walk and then stop walking, if he's walking ahead, which he tends to do. He also has gotten comfortable sniffing. CUDDLE BUG LEVEL Medium – Likes to snuggle when he's in the mood but often stays in his own bed. I would say medium to high. He likes to be on the sofa next to me and loves to be held when we're sitting at the park. I don't allow him to sleep on my bed. He sleeps throughout the night in his crate. JUMPING ON PEOPLE TO SAY HELLO Listens to correction – Only jumps on people they know when really excited, stops with correction. CRATE TRAINING Yep/mostly – Seems comfortable in the crate, may whine a little at first but settles pretty quickly. We use the crate when we leave the pup alone and/or at night. He has adjusted quite well to the crate. He goes in easily, with some mild coaxing at times. He sleeps through the night in the crate with no whining. I will leave him in the crate whenever I step out. Medical status: Healthy as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP and Bordetella vaccines, spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. (For dogs under 4 months old, adopters will need to finish the DHPP vaccine series and administer the Rabies vaccine at 16 weeks of age.) How did this dog end up with Social Tees? Most of our dogs come via partner groups who help us save them from shelters where they are at risk of euthanasia in Tennessee, Los Angeles, and Puerto Rico. There are very few spay/neuter resources there and many more animals in those areas than there are people to adopt them. Rescue groups like ours bring them to the northeast where the desire for pets like these allows us to save their lives. PLEASE NOTE: We cannot guarantee any breed mix, exact age, or full grown size (if the dog is under a year old). We do our best with very educated guesses. This animal is not at the Social Tees office, all are in foster homes. LEARN MORE ABOUT US: socialteesnyc.org and Instagram @socialteesnyc

We're not sure of this guys breed mix, he's a smaller guy with big do features, a stunner! 

If you want to see a video of this dog please click here. 

Expected to be about 35lbs full grown 

This puppy is eligible to join our foster-to-adopt program. Please email fostertoadopt@socialteesnyc.org with the animal’s name in the subject line if you are interested! Want to straight up adopt? Submit an adoption application at socialteesnyc.org

Their Foster Family Says: "Teddy is SO curious! Listens to the wind. Wants to say hi to other dogs (all sizes) and approaches with energy and playful vibes but then retreats in self consciousness and hides behind my legs. He wants to pick up every stick and leaf and parade them around as his new treasures but drops them easily and moves on to the next street-delight. Teddy has learned “sit” and sometimes gets “paw”! He is treat motivated and highly focused on his bones/chew treats for hours. He also LOVES his human (immediately started to treat me like a mama). He wants to unravel his bones while sitting next to me and when I’m standing up and walking about he will follow me around squeaking and chewing his toy. His noises are soooo sweet. Squeaks and whimpers to express delight and rarely barks — only when someone in the hall of my apartment building startles him. He got something sticky stuck to his tail and I was worried that pulling it off he would be upset but no! He was a patient patient; displaying bravery/kindness even as his tail was jostled and pulled. He's a boy with a sweet and gentle soul and would do best with people who are patient as he continues to figure out how to be brave and make friends." 

Level of dog ownership experience required:
INTERMEDIATE – As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day. The adopter must have relevant primary care experience with a similar breed, temperament, and/or energy level. (Primary care experience includes ownership, fostering, or dog sitting as an adult, not a dog you grew up with.) Relevant puppy care experience is a huge plus, but bare minimum the adopter must have TONS of time and patience. Raising a puppy can be a lot of fun, but it’s also  tremendous work. Puppies’ personalities and exercise/stimulation requirements change dramatically between now and when they’re a year old as their bodies and brains develop, so an active lifestyle and the ability to adapt to a pup’s evolving needs are a must. PLEASE DO YOUR OWN BREED RESEARCH to make sure you have a better understanding of the kind of temperament and exercise requirements this dog may have as an adult.

Energy Level:
MEDIUM – Very young puppies sleep and nap a lot, but their energy level skyrockets when they become teens (4 months to around a year). As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 60 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day at a minimum. (This is regardless of dog size – many small breeds were designed for lots of activity and will exhibit unwanted behavior when they’re understimulated.) 

TOLERANCE TO CITY
Adjusting to the city – Spooked easily by loud noises and bustling areas but walks pretty well in quiet areas and probably just needs more time to adjust (may be a puppy or a brand new rescue). Would prefer a home in a calmer part of the city or the suburbs. Teddy is easily spooked by loud cars/trucks/sirens. He can be a little skittish at a passing skateboarder. Ideal home would be somewhere calm Although, I think he needs more time to get acclimated.

POTTY TRAINING
Yes – Few or no accidents. He still relies on wee pads for peeing, as he drinks quite a bit of water. He has learned to go number 2 outside. 

COMFORT LEVEL WITH STRANGERS
Wallflower – Very shy with new people and takes a while to warm up. Afraid when unfamiliar people try to say hi on the street, hides or shrinks back when new people visit the home. Teddy is very timid around strangers. He recoils if a stranger tries to approach him. If a stranger comes to my home, he will bark, but will not approach the person. 

BEHAVIOR WITH CHILDREN (always requires adult supervision)
Maybe for age 12 and up – Is either big and energetic (okay with kids big enough not to get knocked down) or a little skittish (could be comfortable with older children that can be extra gentle) He has moments when he can be mouthy and gets the zoomies. He can be skittish among young children. 

SOCIAL BEHAVIOR WITH OTHER DOGS
Still working on it – Either retreats from other dogs or barks at them/leash reactive. Needs more socialization training or may just be a dog that prefers human company. He is very afraid of dogs larger than him. He shows some interest in smaller dogs, but needs to be trained to approach them calmly. 

MOUTHY BEHAVIOR
Needs training – Is either still in the puppy stage or was never trained. Tries to put their mouth on your hands when playing or needs attention, grabs leash, chews on your personal belongings. Teddy has a propensity to bite hands. I've noticed this occurs after he's energized from a walk. Firm correction usually stops him. He also likes to bite the leash on walks. If left unsupervised, he will try to eat shoes, grabs clothes within reach, eat cardboard, dig in bathroom trashcan.

SEPARATION ANXIETY (Please leave your foster dog home alone every day for at least 20 minutes.)
Adjusting – Might cry for a few minutes when you first leave the house but settles pretty quickly and has no problem being left alone otherwise. I've left him alone for a couple of hours in some cases, and he does whimper, but the eventually settles down with his chew toys. He's always placed in the crate when I leave him alone, so there's no destruction. As he's a puppy, I cannot trust him to roam around my apt alone.

LEASH MANNERS
Getting the hang of it – Probably hasn’t been on a leash much in their life but figuring it out. Might be a mild puller but responds to correction. He's still getting the hang of walking on one's side. He tends to zigzag left to right during walks. He sometimes gets eager and starts pulling ahead. He will walk and then stop walking, if he's walking ahead, which he tends to do. He also has gotten comfortable sniffing.

CUDDLE BUG LEVEL
Medium – Likes to snuggle when he's in the mood but often stays in his own bed. I would say medium to high. He likes to be on the sofa next to me and loves to be held when we're sitting at the park. I don't allow him to sleep on my bed. He sleeps throughout the night in his crate. 

JUMPING ON PEOPLE TO SAY HELLO 
Listens to correction – Only jumps on people they know when really excited, stops with correction.

CRATE TRAINING
Yep/mostly – Seems comfortable in the crate, may whine a little at first but settles pretty quickly. We use the crate when we leave the pup alone and/or at night. He has adjusted quite well to the crate. He goes in easily, with some mild coaxing at times. He sleeps through the night in the crate with no whining. I will leave him in the crate whenever I step out.

Medical status:
Healthy as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP and Bordetella vaccines, spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. (For dogs under 4 months old, adopters will need to finish the DHPP vaccine series and administer the Rabies vaccine at 16 weeks of age.)

How did this dog end up with Social Tees?
Most of our dogs come via partner groups who help us save them from shelters where they are at risk of euthanasia in Tennessee, Los Angeles, and Puerto Rico. There are very few spay/neuter resources there and many more animals in those areas than there are people to adopt them. Rescue groups like ours bring them to the northeast where the desire for pets like these allows us to save their lives. 

PLEASE NOTE: We cannot guarantee any breed mix, exact age, or full grown size (if the dog is under a year old). We do our best with very educated guesses. 

This animal is not at the Social Tees office, all are in foster homes.

EXPERT – As an adult, this dog will need loads of structure and daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 2+ consecutive hours of quick paced movement plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day. The adopter must have relevant primary care experience with a similar breed, temperament, and/or energy level. (Primary care experience includes ownership, fostering, or dog sitting as an adult, not a dog you grew up with.) Relevant puppy care experience is a huge plus, but bare minimum the adopter must have TONS of time and patience. Raising a puppy can be a lot of fun, but it’s also tremendous work. Puppies’ personalities and exercise/stimulation requirements change dramatically between now and when they’re a year old as their bodies and brains develop, so an active lifestyle and the ability to adapt to a pup’s evolving needs are a must. We strongly urge professional dog training with a rewards based trainer from the get go. Adults only or kids ages 8 and up – all puppies go through a mouthy, rambunctious phase and often accidentally hurt children when playing. PLEASE DO YOUR OWN BREED RESEARCH to make sure you have a better understanding of the kind of temperament and exercise requirements this dog may have as an adult.

Energy Level: MEDIUM – Very young puppies sleep and nap a lot, but their energy level skyrockets when they become teens (4 months to around a year). As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day at a minimum. (This is regardless of dog size – many small breeds were designed for lots of activity and will exhibit unwanted behavior when they’re understimulated.) 

Potty trained?
Working on this skill. Puppies under 12 weeks old are often on track with their wee pad skills, but they’re too young to walk outside in public NYC areas yet because they haven’t finished their puppy vaccine series. Puppies older than 12 weeks are usually learning to do their business outside. Potty training takes a lot of patience, consistency, and clean up. 

Social with dogs?
Yes. Some puppies are shy, others are bold, but all have the potential to be taught healthy socializing skills. It’s a huge part of raising a puppy and must be done carefully. How they interact with other dogs depends largely on how their humans help them learn to. 

Social with children?  (ALWAYS requires adult supervision)
Sort of – some puppies enjoy interacting with children, others get easily overwhelmed by their energy and attention. Regardless, most puppies are not a great match for a home with kids under age 8 because they go through intense mouthy play and rambunctious phases and often accidentally hurt young kids while playing. Children must always be monitored and taught to interact with dogs of any age respectfully.  

Social with cats?
Yes. Most puppies have the potential to be friends with a cat. It’s on the adopter to know their cat’s temperament and preferences and to teach their puppy respectful manners. 

Mouthy play: 
High! All puppies go through phases where they chew your stuff and grab your hands, arms, feet… puppies naturally explore the world, play, and test boundaries with their mouths. (It also happens when they’re teething.) Their teeth are super sharp, so it can be a very painful phase for humans and other animals in the home. Proper training, outlets, and socialization are key.

Separation anxiety:
Most puppies have some level of separation anxiety as they learn to self soothe. Often they cry the first 10+ minutes at night or when they are left home alone or in a crate. Consistent training and alone time is crucial.

Leash manners:
None or learning, depending on the puppy’s age. Will need to work on this skill.  

Crate trained?
Probably not. None of our new puppies have been formally trained, but many of our foster parents/adopters choose to crate train so some of the puppies that have been with us for a little while are learning this skill. It can be a great way to keep puppies safe and teach them independence.

Medical status:
Healthy as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP and Bordetella vaccines, spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. (For dogs under 4 months old, adopters will need to finish the DHPP vaccine series and administer the Rabies vaccine at 16 weeks of age.)

How did this dog end up with Social Tees?
Most of our dogs come via partner groups who help us save them from shelters where they are at risk of euthanasia in Tennessee, Los Angeles, and Puerto Rico. There are very few spay/neuter resources there and many more animals in those areas than there are people to adopt them. Rescue groups like ours bring them to the northeast where the desire for pets like these allows us to save their lives. 

PLEASE NOTE: We cannot guarantee any breed mix, exact age, or full grown size (if the dog is under a year old). We do our best with very educated guesses. 

This animal is not at the Social Tees office, all are in foster homes.

Expected to be about 45lbs full grown 

This puppy is eligible to join our foster-to-adopt program. Please email fostertoadopt@socialteesnyc.org with the animal’s name in the subject line if you are interested! Want to straight up adopt? Submit an adoption application at socialteesnyc.org

Level of dog ownership experience required:
INTERMEDIATE – As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day. The adopter must have relevant primary care experience with a similar breed, temperament, and/or energy level. (Primary care experience includes ownership, fostering, or dog sitting as an adult, not a dog you grew up with.) Relevant puppy care experience is a huge plus, but bare minimum the adopter must have TONS of time and patience. Raising a puppy can be a lot of fun, but it’s also  tremendous work. Puppies’ personalities and exercise/stimulation requirements change dramatically between now and when they’re a year old as their bodies and brains develop, so an active lifestyle and the ability to adapt to a pup’s evolving needs are a must. We strongly urge professional dog training with a rewards based trainer from the get go. Adults only or kids ages 8 and up – all puppies go through a mouthy, rambunctious phase and often accidentally hurt children when playing. PLEASE DO YOUR OWN BREED RESEARCH to make sure you have a better understanding of the kind of temperament and exercise requirements this dog may have as an adult.

Energy level:
MEDIUM – Very young puppies sleep and nap a lot, but their energy level skyrockets when they become teens (4 months to around a year). As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day at a minimum. (This is regardless of dog size – many small breeds were designed for lots of activity and will exhibit unwanted behavior when they’re understimulated.) 

Potty trained?
Working on this skill. Puppies under 12 weeks old are often on track with their wee pad skills, but they’re too young to walk outside in public NYC areas yet because they haven’t finished their puppy vaccine series. Puppies older than 12 weeks are usually learning to do their business outside. Potty training takes a lot of patience, consistency, and clean up. 

Social with dogs?
Yes. Some puppies are shy, others are bold, but all have the potential to be taught healthy socializing skills. It’s a huge part of raising a puppy and must be done carefully. How they interact with other dogs depends largely on how their humans help them learn to. 

Social with children?  (ALWAYS requires adult supervision)
Sort of – some puppies enjoy interacting with children, others get easily overwhelmed by their energy and attention. Regardless, most puppies are not a great match for a home with kids under age 8 because they go through intense mouthy play and rambunctious phases and often accidentally hurt young kids while playing. Children must always be monitored and taught to interact with dogs of any age respectfully.  

Social with cats?
Yes. Most puppies have the potential to be friends with a cat. It’s on the adopter to know their cat’s temperament and preferences and to teach their puppy respectful manners. 

Mouthy play: 
High! All puppies go through phases where they chew your stuff and grab your hands, arms, feet… puppies naturally explore the world, play, and test boundaries with their mouths. (It also happens when they’re teething.) Their teeth are super sharp, so it can be a very painful phase for humans and other animals in the home. Proper training, outlets, and socialization are key.

Separation anxiety:
Most puppies have some level of separation anxiety as they learn to self soothe. Often they cry the first 10+ minutes at night or when they are left home alone or in a crate. Consistent training and alone time is crucial.

Leash manners:
None or learning, depending on the puppy’s age. Will need to work on this skill.  

Crate trained?
Probably not. None of our new puppies have been formally trained, but many of our foster parents/adopters choose to crate train so some of the puppies that have been with us for a little while are learning this skill. It can be a great way to keep puppies safe and teach them independence.

Medical status:
Healthy as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP and Bordetella vaccines, spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. (For dogs under 4 months old, adopters will need to finish the DHPP vaccine series and administer the Rabies vaccine at 16 weeks of age.)

How did this dog end up with Social Tees?
Most of our dogs come via partner groups who help us save them from shelters where they are at risk of euthanasia in Tennessee, Los Angeles, and Puerto Rico. There are very few spay/neuter resources there and many more animals in those areas than there are people to adopt them. Rescue groups like ours bring them to the northeast where the desire for pets like these allows us to save their lives. 

PLEASE NOTE: We cannot guarantee any breed mix, exact age, or full grown size (if the dog is under a year old). We do our best with very educated guesses. 

This animal is not at the Social Tees office, all are in foster homes.

pets.name: Lil Bit
pets.description: Lil Bit - 8 years, 11lbs, Chiweenie, Neutered - Our vet estimates him to be anywhere between 5 to 7 and possibly even 8. Please click here to see videos of little bit. His Foster Family Says: "Lil Bit has been the sweetest foster dog we could have asked for. From the moment we picked him up, he has been incredibly sweet, calm, trusting, and well behaved. He gets along wonderfully with our dogs and has such a kind, gentle soul. At home, Lil Bit is calm and affectionate. He loves snuggling with us on the couch and being near his people, but in a gentle, independent way that is never overly needy. He is very quiet and is happy relaxing, sleeping, or watching the world go by from our window sill, one of his favorite spots. His sweet little face and adorable snaggle tooth are just as charming as his affectionate personality! Lil Bit is also incredibly easy to care for. He is fully house trained and enjoys one longer walk each day along with a couple of shorter walks. He is not reactive on walks. He approaches the world with a wonderful sense of curiously and trust, and really enjoys meeting other dogs and people he passes on walks." Level of dog ownership experience needed: FLEXIBLE – We predict this dog will be low on the challenge scale with regard to exercise and mental stimulation requirements, but seniors tend to need a lot of help and understanding when it comes to lifestyle and veterinary issues. Seniors usually need quiet, calm environments and routines and do not do well with a lot of bustle, change, and rambunctious movement (kids and young playful dogs, for instance). This dog’s adopter will need to be prepared for senior health challenges, which means frequent vet visits and very expensive veterinary bills. (An annual senior blood panel alone costs around $500 in NYC.) Senior care can also take an emotional toll on their humans. Adopting a mature pup is a wonderful thing to do, but it can also be difficult. Energy level: LOWER – Pretty chill indoors and won’t demand endless amounts of stimulation and exercise but still needs a few short walks a day (10-30 min each) for potty breaks and to stretch their legs TOLERANCE TO CITY Adjusting to the city – Spooked easily by loud noises and bustling areas but walks pretty well in quiet areas and probably just needs more time to adjust (may be a puppy or a brand new rescue). He is sometimes startled by random loud noises but has been able to get around the city, even louder parts, fine. We do live in a more calm part of Brooklyn but he did go on the Subway for the first time yesterday and was totally fine and not scared at all. POTTY TRAINING Yes – Few or no accidents COMFORT LEVEL WITH STRANGERS Social butterfly – Wants to be friends with everyone who walks by, loves anyone who will stop to say hello. BEHAVIOR WITH CHILDREN (always requires adult supervision) Yes for most ages – very confident, gentle, low energy, tolerant, not mouthy SOCIAL BEHAVIOR WITH OTHER DOGS Yes – Good with most other dogs (sizes, breeds, etc.) as far as we know and enjoys socializing with other canines RESPECTFUL BEHAVIOR WITH OTHER ANIMALS (cats, small pets, etc.) Yes – Seems to get along with cats etc., either tries to play with them or is mostly uninterested MOUTHY BEHAVIOR Past this stage– Little to no interest in chewing on stuff or putting things in their mouth that aren’t food. Doesn’t try to chew on hands, feet, etc. during playtime SEPARATION ANXIETY Adjusting – Might cry for a few minutes when you first leave the house but settles pretty quickly and has no problem being left alone otherwise. LEASH MANNERS Old Pro – Doesn’t pull hard or need much direction. CUDDLE BUG LEVEL Medium – Likes to snuggle when he's in the mood but often stays in his own bed JUMPING ON PEOPLE TO SAY HELLO Calm Greetings – Doesn’t jump up on people or dogs. Always all four on the floor. CRATE TRAINING Don't use it - We only tried crating him once and he was whimpering a lot so we let him out. We didn't find the need to keep him in there because he has been very well behaved. Medical status: Healthy for their age as far as we know. Lil Bit - 8 years, 11lbs, Chiweenie, Neutered - Our vet estimates him to be anywhere between 5 to 7 and possibly even 8. 

Please click here to see videos of little bit. 

His Foster Family Says: "Lil Bit has been the sweetest foster dog we could have asked for. From the moment we picked him up, he has been incredibly sweet, calm, trusting, and well behaved. He gets along wonderfully with our dogs and has such a kind, gentle soul. At home, Lil Bit is calm and affectionate. He loves snuggling with us on the couch and being near his people, but in a gentle, independent way that is never overly needy. He is very quiet and is happy relaxing, sleeping, or watching the world go by from our window sill, one of his favorite spots. His sweet little face and adorable snaggle tooth are just as charming as his affectionate personality! Lil Bit is also incredibly easy to care for. He is fully house trained and enjoys one longer walk each day along with a couple of shorter walks. He is not reactive on walks. He approaches the world with a wonderful sense of curiously and trust, and really enjoys meeting other dogs and people he passes on walks."

Level of dog ownership experience needed:
FLEXIBLE – We predict this dog will be low on the challenge scale with regard to exercise and mental stimulation requirements, but seniors tend to need a lot of help and understanding when it comes to lifestyle and veterinary issues. Seniors usually need quiet, calm environments and routines and do not do well with a lot of bustle, change, and rambunctious movement (kids and young playful dogs, for instance). This dog’s adopter will need to be prepared for senior health challenges, which means frequent vet visits and very expensive veterinary bills. (An annual senior blood panel alone costs around $500 in NYC.) Senior care can also take an emotional toll on their humans. Adopting a mature pup is a wonderful thing to do, but it can also be difficult. 

Energy level:
LOWER – Pretty chill indoors and won’t demand endless amounts of stimulation and exercise but still needs a few short walks a day (10-30 min each) for potty breaks and to stretch their legs

TOLERANCE TO CITY
Adjusting to the city – Spooked easily by loud noises and bustling areas but walks pretty well in quiet areas and probably just needs more time to adjust (may be a puppy or a brand new rescue). He is sometimes startled by random loud noises but has been able to get around the city, even louder parts, fine. We do live in a more calm part of Brooklyn but he did go on the Subway for the first time yesterday and was totally fine and not scared at all. 

POTTY TRAINING
Yes – Few or no accidents 

COMFORT LEVEL WITH STRANGERS
Social butterfly – Wants to be friends with everyone who walks by, loves anyone who will stop to say hello. 

BEHAVIOR WITH CHILDREN (always requires adult supervision)
Yes for most ages – very confident, gentle, low energy, tolerant, not mouthy 

SOCIAL BEHAVIOR WITH OTHER DOGS
Yes – Good with most other dogs (sizes, breeds, etc.) as far as we know and enjoys socializing with other canines

RESPECTFUL BEHAVIOR WITH OTHER ANIMALS (cats, small pets, etc.)
Yes – Seems to get along with cats etc., either tries to play with them or is mostly uninterested

MOUTHY BEHAVIOR
Past this stage– Little to no interest in chewing on stuff or putting things in their mouth that aren’t food. Doesn’t try to chew on hands, feet, etc. during playtime

SEPARATION ANXIETY
Adjusting – Might cry for a few minutes when you first leave the house but settles pretty quickly and has no problem being left alone otherwise. 

LEASH MANNERS
Old Pro – Doesn’t pull hard or need much direction. 

CUDDLE BUG LEVEL
Medium – Likes to snuggle when he's in the mood but often stays in his own bed 

JUMPING ON PEOPLE TO SAY HELLO
Calm Greetings – Doesn’t jump up on people or dogs. Always all four on the floor. 

CRATE TRAINING
Don't use it -  We only tried crating him once and he was whimpering a lot so we let him out. We didn't find the need to keep him in there because he has been very well behaved.

Medical status:
Healthy for their age as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP, Bordetella, and Rabies vaccines; heartworm tested if coming from Tennessee or Puerto Rico; spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. Adopters will need to be ready for senior care – at a minimum, that will be annual checkups including senior bloodwork and a dental post adoption (most senior rescues need one).

How did this dog end up with Social Tees?
Most of our dogs come via partner groups who help us save them from shelters where they are at risk of euthanasia in Tennessee, Los Angeles, and Puerto Rico. There are very few spay/neuter resources there and many more animals in those areas than there are people to adopt them. Rescue groups like ours bring them to the northeast where the desire for pets like these allows us to save their lives.

Please email fostertoadopt@socialteesnyc.org with the animal’s name in the subject line if you are interested! Want to straight up adopt? Submit an adoption application a t socialteesnyc.org Thier Foster Family Says: "Elroy is truly one of the happiest and most lovable pups ever. I would definitely consider him a “Velcro dog.” He loves being around his people and will follow you around the house, checking in throughout the day for some love and attention. Every time you walk past him, he will expect to be pet, preferably with his belly up! He absolutely LOVES people. If he could have a “Please Pet Me” sign attached to him, he would. He is the definition of a social butterfly and loves meeting new people and dogs.Elroy especially enjoys meeting smaller dogs, but he does well with dogs of all sizes. He can just be a little more cautious when meeting bigger dogs at first. He also does not seem to realize that he is a big dog! Submit an adoption application a t socialteesnyc.org Thier Foster Dad Says: " Jasmine is a super chill, friendly, go-with-the-flow dog who seems happy pretty much anywhere. She loves people, other dogs, walks, toys, cuddling, being outside, and hanging out at home. She may not have gone on regular walks before, so we’ve been easing her into a normal routine. As she gets used to it and builds up some stamina, I think she’ll happily walk for as long as you’d like. For now, she comes home and immediately takes a well-earned nap. She’s calm and comfortable at home, including when she’s left alone, although she’s definitely a glutton for attention when you’re around. Also needs significant socializing opportunities outside the home and mental stimulation at home like tricks training practice, chew items, and puzzle toys. (This is regardless of dog size – many small breeds were designed for lots of activity and will exhibit unwanted behavior when they’re understimulated.) TOLERANCE TO CITY: City pup. COMFORT LEVEL WITH STRANGERS: Social butterfly. She loves people and wants to make friends with pretty much everyone. She’s definitely not a guard dog. BEHAVIOR WITH CHILDREN: Yes for most ages, based on her previous foster’s experience. I haven’t personally seen her around kids, but her previous foster said she did well with them. SOCIAL BEHAVIOR WITH OTHER DOGS: Yes. She’s super friendly and playful with other dogs. She can come on a little strong at first, especially with smaller dogs, because she’s excited to sniff them and say hello. INTERMEDIATE – As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day. Adjusting to the city – would love a home in a calm area 

POTTY TRAINING
Working on this skill. BEHAVIOR WITH CHILDREN (always requires adult supervision)

Not sure – Wants to chase squirrels and birds so may not be a good match for a home with cats, rabbits, etc.

Working on it – Is respectful of hands, feet, etc. but likes to chew on things they’re not supposed to like shoes, furniture, etc.

Ocean is doing great being left home alone now. Most puppies have some level of separation anxiety as they learn to self soothe. Often they cry the first 10+ minutes at night or when they are left home alone or in a crate. Consistent training and alone time is crucial.

Getting the hang of it – Probably hasn’t been on a leash much in their life but figuring it out. Might be a mild puller but responds to correction. 

CUDDLE BUG LEVEL
Medium – Likes to snuggle when he's in the mood but often stays in his own bed 

JUMPING ON PEOPLE TO SAY HELLO
Listens to correction – Only jumps on people they know when really excited, stops with correction.

Yep/mostly – Seems comfortable in the crate, may whine a little at first but settles pretty quickly. We use the crate when we leave the pup alone and/or at night.

Healthy as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP and Bordetella vaccines, spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. (For dogs under 4 months old, adopters will need to finish the DHPP vaccine series and administer the Rabies vaccine at 16 weeks of age.)

This puppy is eligible to join our foster-to-adopt program. Please email fostertoadopt@socialteesnyc.org with the animal’s name in the subject line if you are interested! Want to straight up adopt? She's just a more sensitve girl. But once she's had time to settle in - there's NO stopping her - she's cuddly and the most fun." Thier Foster Parent Says: " At 10 months, a whopping 15 pounds, and the longest limbs and tiniest head, Snug is the silliest proportioned puppy I've ever had the honor of meeting. Her personality aligns with that silliness too. From collecting (but not chewing!) my shoes to build a fort to using her paws like a human to smack me for attention, Snug is one odd ball. She's super easily entertained by cardboard and plays well alone if given a bouncy ball or just a great view out the window. That girl could people watch for days. But that's not to say she doesn't absolutely love her daily playdates with her doggy friends in the building. Snug can be a little overwhelming for smaller more timid dogs because of her lanky arms that are always flailing around, but she never becomes aggressive. She also loves her human (and humans in general). Sometimes she can be a little hesitant to meet men for the first time, but that goes away as soon as you have a treat in hand. She is a snuggle bug to any and all people who walk through my door. She loves to get really comfortable on you, laying her head right below yours and it's just the sweetest thing. Snug listens well and learns quickly, knowing to sit to wait for her food and rarely missing the peed pad these days. Regarding city life, she's not quite there yet. She's getting used to outside walks, but would prefer a quieter neighborhood without bikers riding around playing pink pony club and heavy foot traffic. She really needs a home that loves to play, cuddle, and bonus! has a yard for her to dig in (right now she digs my pillow and couch, but that just doesn't hit the same you know?)" Snug - 10 months (as of 8/31) and 15lbs, Beagle Mix, Spayed 
Mostly full grown - might gain a tiny bit more weight - 1lb to 2lbs 

Want to see a video of this Snug please click here!

This puppy is eligible to join our foster-to-adopt program. Please email fostertoadopt@socialteesnyc.org with the animal’s name in the subject line if you are interested! Want to straight up adopt? Submit an adoption application at socialteesnyc.org

Our Team Says: "Snug takes a little bit of time to warm up to new people. But she's a sweet girl and so fun. She prefers a home in a calmer area. She's just a more sensitve girl. But once she's had time to settle in - there's NO stopping her - she's cuddly and the most fun." 

Thier Foster Parent Says: "At 10 months, a whopping 15 pounds, and the longest limbs and tiniest head, Snug is the silliest proportioned puppy I've ever had the honor of meeting. Her personality aligns with that silliness too. From collecting (but not chewing!) my shoes to build a fort to using her paws like a human to smack me for attention, Snug is one odd ball. She's super easily entertained by cardboard and plays well alone if given a bouncy ball or just a great view out the window. That girl could people watch for days. But that's not to say she doesn't absolutely love her daily playdates with her doggy friends in the building. Snug can be a little overwhelming for smaller more timid dogs because of her lanky arms that are always flailing around, but she never becomes aggressive. She also loves her human (and humans in general). Sometimes she can be a little hesitant to meet men for the first time, but that goes away as soon as you have a treat in hand. She is a snuggle bug to any and all people who walk through my door. She loves to get really comfortable on you, laying her head right below yours and it's just the sweetest thing. Snug listens well and learns quickly, knowing to sit to wait for her food and rarely missing the peed pad these days. Regarding city life, she's not quite there yet. She's getting used to outside walks, but would prefer a quieter neighborhood without bikers riding around playing pink pony club and heavy foot traffic. She really needs a home that loves to play, cuddle, and bonus! has a yard for her to dig in (right now she digs my pillow and couch, but that just doesn't hit the same you know?)"

Level of dog ownership experience required:
INTERMEDIATE – As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day. The adopter must have relevant primary care experience with a similar breed, temperament, and/or energy level. (Primary care experience includes ownership, fostering, or dog sitting as an adult, not a dog you grew up with.) Relevant puppy care experience is a huge plus, but bare minimum the adopter must have TONS of time and patience. Raising a puppy can be a lot of fun, but it’s also  tremendous work. Puppies’ personalities and exercise/stimulation requirements change dramatically between now and when they’re a year old as their bodies and brains develop, so an active lifestyle and the ability to adapt to a pup’s evolving needs are a must. We strongly urge professional dog training with a rewards based trainer from the get go. Adults only or kids ages 8 and up – all puppies go through a mouthy, rambunctious phase and often accidentally hurt children when playing. PLEASE DO YOUR OWN BREED RESEARCH to make sure you have a better understanding of the kind of temperament and exercise requirements this dog may have as an adult.

Energy level:
MEDIUM – Very young puppies sleep and nap a lot, but their energy level skyrockets when they become teens (4 months to around a year). As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day at a minimum. (This is regardless of dog size – many small breeds were designed for lots of activity and will exhibit unwanted behavior when they’re understimulated.) 

TOLERANCE TO CITY
Calm Areas Are Best– Spooked easily by loud noises and bustling areas but walks pretty well in quiet areas 

POTTY TRAINING
Yes – 100% accurarcy on pee pads, needs a calm neighborhood to do her business outside. 

COMFORT LEVEL WITH STRANGERS
In between bean – Fine with meeting new people but not particularly interested, kind of shy in busy social situations like a gathering or a packed day in the park.

Social with dogs?
Yes. Some puppies are shy, others are bold, but all have the potential to be taught healthy socializing skills. It’s a huge part of raising a puppy and must be done carefully. How they interact with other dogs depends largely on how their humans help them learn to. 

Social with children?  (ALWAYS requires adult supervision)
Sort of – some puppies enjoy interacting with children, others get easily overwhelmed by their energy and attention. Regardless, most puppies are not a great match for a home with kids under age 8 because they go through intense mouthy play and rambunctious phases and often accidentally hurt young kids while playing. Children must always be monitored and taught to interact with dogs of any age respectfully.  

Social with cats?
Yes. Most puppies have the potential to be friends with a cat. It’s on the adopter to know their cat’s temperament and preferences and to teach their puppy respectful manners. 

MOUTHY BEHAVIOR
Past this stage– Little to no interest in chewing on stuff or putting things in their mouth that aren’t food. Doesn’t try to chew on hands, feet, etc. during playtime

SEPARATION ANXIETY (Please leave your foster dog home alone every day for at least 20 minutes.)
Adjusting – Might cry for a few minutes when you first leave the house but settles pretty quickly and has no problem being left alone otherwise.

LEASH MANNERS
Getting the hang of it – Probably hasn’t been on a leash much in their life but figuring it out. Might be a mild puller but responds to correction

CUDDLE BUG LEVEL
Medium – Likes to snuggle when she's in the mood but often stays in her own bed

JUMPING ON PEOPLE TO SAY HELLO
Calm Greetings – Doesn’t jump up on people or dogs. Always all four on th

CRATE TRAINING
yep/mostly – Seems comfortable in the crate, may whine a little at first but settles pretty quickly. We use the crate when we leave the pup alone and/or at night.

Medical status:
Healthy as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP and Bordetella vaccines, spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. (For dogs under 4 months old, adopters will need to finish the DHPP vaccine series and administer the Rabies vaccine at 16 weeks of age.)

How did this dog end up with Social Tees?
Most of our dogs come via partner groups who help us save them from shelters where they are at risk of euthanasia in Tennessee, Los Angeles, and Puerto Rico. There are very few spay/neuter resources there and many more animals in those areas than there are people to adopt them. Rescue groups like ours bring them to the northeast where the desire for pets like these allows us to save their lives. 

PLEASE NOTE: We cannot guarantee any breed mix, exact age, or full grown size (if the dog is under a year old). We do our best with very educated guesses. 

This animal is not at the Social Tees office, all are in foster homes.

Relevant puppy care experience is a huge plus, but bare minimum the adopter must have TONS of time and patience. Raising a puppy can be a lot of fun, but it’s also  tremendous work. Puppies’ personalities and exercise/stimulation requirements change dramatically between now and when they’re a year old as their bodies and brains develop, so an active lifestyle and the ability to adapt to a pup’s evolving needs are a must. We strongly urge professional dog training with a rewards based trainer from the get go. Adults only or kids ages 8 and up – all puppies go through a mouthy, rambunctious phase and often accidentally hurt children when playing. PLEASE DO YOUR OWN BREED RESEARCH to make sure you have a better understanding of the kind of temperament and exercise requirements this dog may have as an adult.

**Energy level:  

MEDIUM** – She is pretty chill indoors, sleeps a lot, and doesn't demand constant stimulation. She enjoys walks but is not extremely high-energy.

**Tolerance to the city:** She is easily spooked by loud noises, bustling areas, and new things. She does much better in quieter areas or places she's been to a lot. She needs time to build confidence. A calmer part of the city or suburbs would probably be ideal.

**Potty trained?** Very few accidents. She always pees outside and consistently poops outside on walks. She has never peed in the house and has only pooped inside twice. She will chew through pee pads.

**Comfort level with strangers:** She is shy and timid with unfamiliar people who come with a lot of energy. But in seconds, if a person is calm with her, she's immediately comfortable and seeks their affection. She jumps on people she knows when saying hello, but not strangers.

**Social with dogs?**She is gentle with other animals and does well around them. She is not interested in rough play. Overly excited animals will scare her.

**Social with children?  (ALWAYS requires adult supervision)**She is extremely gentle and calm with children and is not mouthy. She does not nip or bite. Adult supervision is, of course, still required.

**Social with cats?**She is gentle with other animals and does not display aggressive or overly excitable behavior around them.

**Mouthy play**: One of her funniest quirks is that she likes to collect socks! She doesn't seem interested in destroying things other than paper and pee pads. She is not mouthy at all. She does not nip, bite, grab hands, or use her mouth during play. She doesn't lick really at all. She loves to sniff and sit next to people.

**Separation anxiety:** Her biggest challenge right now is separation anxiety. She can wait at the front door for as much as an hour. She does not destroy things when left alone, but she becomes sad/pouty and struggles with being separated from her people. She would benefit from continued separation-anxiety training.

**Leash manners**: She is a mild puller when she smells something new. When she is scared, she will not walk at all. When confident in a familiar area, she doesn’t pull at all.

**Cuddle bug level:** She doesn’t put herself in people's laps, but she loves sitting next to her people and being close. She will always go to rooms with people and nap almost immediately.

**Crate trained?**She hates the crate and is not currently comfortable being confined in one. She will need continued positive crate training. I have taught her to sleep in her dog bed, but she can only do so if someone is in the room with her.

**Medical status:**  

Healthy as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP and Bordetella vaccines, spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. (For dogs under 4 months old, adopters will need to finish the DHPP vaccine series and administer the Rabies vaccine at 16 weeks of age.)

**How did this dog end up with Social Tees?**  

Most of our dogs come via partner groups who help us save them from shelters where they are at risk of euthanasia in Tennessee, Los Angeles, and Puerto Rico. There are very few spay/neuter resources there and many more animals in those areas than there are people to adopt them. Rescue groups like ours bring them to the northeast where the desire for pets like these allows us to save their lives. 

PLEASE NOTE: We cannot guarantee any breed mix, exact age, or full grown size (if the dog is under a year old). We do our best with very educated guesses. 

This animal is not at the Social Tees office, all are in foster homes.

The equine traits make him a tender being, very herd oriented, never happier than when in an open green space, easily spooked. It makes me sad that he’s the type of dog most people look past or don’t have the patience for. I myself was pretty annoyed when I got stuck with him. He had no place to go, but I couldn’t let such a glum and sensitive dog go to boarding. Within two weeks, I was ready to die for him. At his core he’s a giant lover. He adores my dog, is good with cats, and has been the most wonderful ‘uncle’ to the puppies we’ve fostered. He gives great snuggles, and he wouldn’t hurt a fly. I think someone hurt him in the past, which is why he’s terrified. I swung my foot at him by accident once as I tripped, and it took him 24 hours to trust me again. Prozac has helped reduce his fear, but he’s still learning. Hank needs a home outside the city with another dog. He’s respectful of your stuff, fine home alone, potty trained, and quiet. He doesn’t sleep with us, but every morning he jumps into bed to give me and my dog morning kisses and cuddles. He can be a part of our family as long as he needs to but we really hope to get him into a rural setting.”

BEGINNER: This means we predict this dog will be low on the challenge scale due to its breed/age combo. Potentially a good fit for someone who has relevant dog care experience (fostering, dog sitting) and is looking to adopt their first pup.

MEDIUM: Needs a daily 60-90 minute walk or window of quick paced exercise (minimum) in addition to potty break strolls (10-30 min each). POTTY TRAINING
Yes – Few or no accidents

COMFORT LEVEL WITH STRANGERS
Wallflower – Very shy with new people and takes a while to warm up. Afraid when unfamiliar people try to say hi on the street, hides or shrinks back when new people visit the home. 

BEHAVIOR WITH CHILDREN (always requires adult supervision)
Maybe for age 12 and up – Is either big and energetic (okay with kids big enough not to get knocked down) or a little skittish (could be comfortable with older children that can be extra gentle) 

SOCIAL BEHAVIOR WITH OTHER DOGS
Great with other dogs–  fine to share a home with another dog 

MOUTHY BEHAVIOR
Past this stage– Little to no interest in chewing on stuff or putting things in their mouth that aren’t food. Doesn’t try to chew on hands, feet, etc. during playtime

SEPARATION ANXIETY
Past this stage – Completely fine being left home alone. Doesn’t cry or exhibit destructive behavior when you leave the apartment or house. 

LEASH MANNERS
Old Pro – Doesn’t pull hard or need much direction. 

CUDDLE BUG LEVEL
Medium – Likes to snuggle when he's in the mood but often stays in his own bed 

JUMPING ON PEOPLE TO SAY HELLO
Calm Greetings – Doesn’t jump up on people or dogs. Always all four on the floor. 

CRATE TRAINING
Yep/mostly – Seems comfortable in the crate, may whine a little at first but settles pretty quickly. We use the crate when we leave the pup alone and/or at night. 

Medical status:
Healthy as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP, Bordetella, and Rabies vaccines; heartworm tested if coming from the South or Puerto Rico ; spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake

Cody was treated for HW and is doing great and finally got to come NYC to find his forever family. He could do really well with another calm, confident pup who is happy to snooze alongside him and give him his space. He needs someone patient who isn’t looking for immediate affection or a dog who will be in their lap on day one. Due to this these pups are on the shyer side and need patient people who will give them time to get used to normal life. They are very sweet dogs: just need more time and patience. Cody was treated for HW and is doing great and finally got to come NYC to find his forever family. Cody would do best in a home with another dog, he needs it for his confidence, has never not lived with another pup"

**Thier Foster Family Says:** "Cody is a sweet angel boy and anyone would be lucky to have him in their lives. He is potty trained and will hold it until he’s outside - he has never had an accident! Despite his incredibly heartbreaking start to life, he’s not letting it define what’s next for him. He walks like a dream by your side despite his fearful tendencies and is happiest relaxing during the day (very Chihuahua of him!) as long as he gets his three walks and an additional potty break before bed. We’ve found that one or two longer walks a day really help him work through some of his anxiety and fear, and he seems to genuinely enjoy exploring the world from the safety of your side. He’s gotten along well with our other pup but definitely has a calm, chill personality. He mostly ignores other dogs and their bad behavior and is a pretty great influence! Coming from a hoarding situation, we think he’s still quite desensitized to both people and dogs and tends to use avoidance as a way to cope when he’s unsure. He could do really well with another calm, confident pup who is happy to snooze alongside him and give him his space. He’s smart, curious, gentle, and we have a feeling there’s so much more personality waiting to come out as he begins to understand that he’s safe. He needs someone patient who isn’t looking for immediate affection or a dog who will be in their lap on day one. What he needs is someone willing to let him move at his own pace and celebrate the little victories along the way. Yes, but we don’t know to what degree yet. Some like to wrestle with every passing pup, others can coexist well but prefer to keep to themselves. We’ll learn more soon.

Not sure yet! Some breed mixes that are generally NOT great matches for homes with cats include large hounds, huskies, and shepherds.

We’re not sure yet, but we try to err on the side of caution. Respectful kids ages 8 and up are probably a safe bet. Children must always be monitored and taught to interact with dogs of any age carefully.

Wallflower, takeas a long time to warm up to new people.

pets.description: John - 12 weeks & 10lbs (as of 7/22), Collie/Terrier, Neutered Estimated to be about 35lbs full grown If you would like to see a video of this dog please click HERE! This puppy is eligible to join our foster-to-adopt program. Please email fostertoadopt@socialteesnyc.org with the animal’s name in the subject line if you are interested! Want to straight up adopt? Submit an adoption application a t socialteesnyc.org Level of dog ownership experience required: INTERMEDIATE – As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day. The adopter must have relevant primary care experience with a similar breed, temperament, and/or energy level. (Primary care experience includes ownership, fostering, or dog sitting as an adult, not a dog you grew up with.) Relevant puppy care experience is a huge plus, but bare minimum the adopter must have TONS of time and patience. Raising a puppy can be a lot of fun, but it’s also tremendous work. Puppies’ personalities and exercise/stimulation requirements change dramatically between now and when they’re a year old as their bodies and brains develop, so an active lifestyle and the ability to adapt to a pup’s evolving needs are a must. We strongly urge professional dog training with a rewards based trainer from the get go. Adults only or kids ages 8 and up – all puppies go through a mouthy, rambunctious phase and often accidentally hurt children when playing. PLEASE DO YOUR OWN BREED RESEARCH to make sure you have a better understanding of the kind of temperament and exercise requirements this dog may have as an adult. Energy level: MEDIUM – Very young puppies sleep and nap a lot, but their energy level skyrockets when they become teens (4 months to around a year). As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day at a minimum. (This is regardless of dog size – many small breeds were designed for lots of activity and will exhibit unwanted behavior when they’re understimulated.) Potty trained? Working on this skill. Puppies under 12 weeks old are often on track with their wee pad skills, but they’re too young to walk outside in public NYC areas yet because they haven’t finished their puppy vaccine series. Puppies older than 12 weeks are usually learning to do their business outside. Potty training takes a lot of patience, consistency, and clean up. Social with dogs? Yes. Some puppies are shy, others are bold, but all have the potential to be taught healthy socializing skills. It’s a huge part of raising a puppy and must be done carefully. How they interact with other dogs depends largely on how their humans help them learn to. Social with children? (ALWAYS requires adult supervision) Sort of – some puppies enjoy interacting with children, others get easily overwhelmed by their energy and attention. Regardless, most puppies are not a great match for a home with kids under age 8 because they go through intense mouthy play and rambunctious phases and often accidentally hurt young kids while playing. Children must always be monitored and taught to interact with dogs of any age respectfully. Social with cats? Yes. Most puppies have the potential to be friends with a cat. It’s on the adopter to know their cat’s temperament and preferences and to teach their puppy respectful manners. Mouthy play: High! All puppies go through phases where they chew your stuff and grab your hands, arms, feet… puppies naturally explore the world, play, and test boundaries with their mouths. (It also happens when they’re teething.) Their teeth are super sharp, so it can be a very painful phase for humans and other animals in the home. Proper training, outlets, and socialization are key. Separation anxiety: Most puppies have some level of separation anxiety as they learn to self soothe. Often they cry the first 10+ minutes at night or when they are left home alone or in a crate. Consistent training and alone time is crucial. Leash manners: None or learning, depending on the puppy’s age. Will need to work on this skill. Crate trained? Probably not. None of our new puppies have been formally trained, but many of our foster parents/adopters choose to crate train so some of the puppies that have been with us for a little while are learning this skill. It can be a great way to keep puppies safe and teach them independence. Medical status: Healthy as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP and Bordetella vaccines, spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. (For dogs under 4 months old, adopters will need to finish the DHPP vaccine series and administer the Rabies vaccine at 16 weeks of age.) How did this dog end up with Social Tees? Most of our dogs come via partner groups who help us save them from shelters where they are at risk of euthanasia in Tennessee, Los Angeles, and Puerto Rico. There are very few spay/neuter resources there and many more animals in those areas than there are people to adopt them. Rescue groups like ours bring them to the northeast where the desire for pets like these allows us to save their lives. PLEASE NOTE: We cannot guarantee any breed mix, exact age, or full grown size (if the dog is under a year old). We do our best with very educated guesses. This animal is not at the Social Tees office, all are in foster homes. LEARN MORE ABOUT US: socialteesnyc.org and Instagram @socialteesnyc

pets.description: Jack - 8 months & 35lbs, Lab Mix, Neutered Our Team Says: Jack is a sensitive dog and needs a home outside of the city. He can not be adopted out to a home in the city. Thier Foster Parent Says: " Jack is a wallflower with a heart of kindness—a gentle soul with the most irresistible puppy dog eyes you've ever seen. This sweet boy may take a little time to warm up, but once he does, you'll have the most devoted companion by your side. Jack is a classic "slow to trust, loyal forever" kind of pup. He's still learning that the world is a safe and wonderful place, and he's looking for a patient family to show him the ropes. The good news? He's incredibly treat-motivated, which makes training a breeze and bonding even easier. Once Jack feels comfortable, his true personality shines through. He loves nothing more than curling up right next to you for cozy snuggles. He's also discovered the joy of playing in the snow—watching him romp around outside is pure happiness! While he sometimes needs a little encouragement to head out the door, he's always glad he did once he's exploring the great outdoors. Jack has a wonderful temperament and gets along beautifully with his foster siblings—Addy the dog and Socks the cat—so he'd do well in a home with other gentle pets who can help him come out of his shell. If you're looking for a sweet, snuggly pup who will blossom with a little love and patience, Jack is waiting to steal your heart" ENERGY LEVEL High – Needs a daily 2-hour (or longer) window of quick paced exercise each morning in addition to potty break strolls (10-30 min each). May also need another 40+ minute walk in the afternoon as well as significant opportunities to socialize outside the home and engage in mental stimulation activities at home like tricks training practice, chew items, and puzzle toys. (This is regardless of dog size – many small breeds were designed for lots of activity and will exhibit unwanted behavior when they’re under-stimulated.) TOLERANCE TO CITY Country mouse – Needs a home outside of the city, suburbs or beyond. Terrified of walks, barely wants to move and shakes a lot, eager to get back home (may be a puppy or a brand new rescue). POTTY TRAINING Yes – Few or no accidents COMFORT LEVEL WITH STRANGERS Wallflowe r – Very shy with new people and takes a while to warm up. Afraid when unfamiliar people try to say hi on the street, hides or shrinks back when new people visit the home. BEHAVIOR WITH CHILDREN (always requires adult supervision) Yes for most ages – very confident, gentle, low energy, tolerant, not mouthy SOCIAL BEHAVIOR WITH OTHER DOGS Mostly – Generally good with other dogs but may be selective (scared of big dogs or plays too rough for small dogs, for example) RESPECTFUL BEHAVIOR WITH OTHER ANIMALS (cats, small pets, etc.) Not sure – Wants to chase squirrels and birds so may not be a good match for a home with cats, rabbits, etc. MOUTHY BEHAVIOR Working on it – Is respectful of hands, feet, etc. but likes to chew on things they’re not supposed to like shoes, furniture, etc. SEPARATION ANXIETY Past this stage – Completely fine being left home alone. Doesn’t cry or exhibit destructive behavior when you leave the apartment or house. As long as you aren’t home while in the crate he won’t cry or bark. LEASH MANNERS Getting the hang of it – Probably hasn’t been on a leash much in their life but figuring it out. Might be a mild puller but responds to correction. CUDDLE BUG LEVEL High – Wants to be in your lap pretty much all the time JUMPING ON PEOPLE TO SAY HELLO Calm Greetings – Doesn’t jump up on people or dogs. Always all four on the floor. pets.description: Dani - 10 months & 32lbs (as of 7/14), Collie/Sheltie Mix, Spayed Expected full grown size around 35lbs Wan to see vidoes of her? Please click here . Our Team Says: This dog needs a home in the burbs - yard and calm area is her vibe. She can not do city life. Great with other dogs - would love a dog to play with. This puppy is eligible to join our foster-to-adopt program. Please email fostertoadopt@socialteesnyc.org with the animal’s name in the subject line if you are interested! Want to straight up adopt? Submit an adoption application a t socialteesnyc.org Her Foster Mom Says : "Dani is going to be someone's prize. She's really beautiful, really fun, with just a pinch of naughty. If you're as herder obessed as we are - this girl fits all of the boxes: smart, agile as hell, fast and can do cardio for days. Dani loves other dogs. Loves her humans in the classic non-needy herder way: she won't smoother you but does enjoy a cuddle on her terms. Her ideal home is ready to keep up with her - long walks - fetch in the yard. She really loves to play with toys, it's really cute! Dani's naughty side comes out when it comes to counters - this girl is fast and sneaky - so be alert. She's eager to learn and to please - super food motivated! She's a grea work from home buddy as long as you start the day off right with a long walk or some proper off leash time. (Primary care experience includes ownership, fostering, or dog sitting as an adult, not a dog you grew up with.) Puppies’ personalities and exercise/stimulation requirements change dramatically between now and when they’re a year old as their bodies and brains develop, so an active lifestyle and the ability to adapt to a pup’s evolving needs are a must. We strongly urge professional dog training with a rewards based trainer from the get go. Adults only or kids ages 8 and up – all puppies go through a mouthy, rambunctious phase and often accidentally hurt children when playing. Loves her humans in the classic non-needy herder way: she won't smoother you but does enjoy a cuddle on her terms. Her ideal home is ready to keep up with her - long walks - fetch in the yard. She really loves to play with toys, it's really cute! Dani's naughty side comes out when it comes to counters - this girl is fast and sneaky - so be alert. She's eager to learn and to please - super food motivated! She's a grea work from home buddy as long as you start the day off right with a long walk or some proper off leash time. Whoever ends up with this girl is super lucky!"

INTERMEDIATE – As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day. The adopter must have relevant primary care experience with a similar breed, temperament, and/or energy level. (Primary care experience includes ownership, fostering, or dog sitting as an adult, not a dog you grew up with.) Relevant puppy care experience is a huge plus, but bare minimum the adopter must have TONS of time and patience. Raising a puppy can be a lot of fun, but it’s also  tremendous work. Puppies’ personalities and exercise/stimulation requirements change dramatically between now and when they’re a year old as their bodies and brains develop, so an active lifestyle and the ability to adapt to a pup’s evolving needs are a must. Energy level:
MEDIUM – Very young puppies sleep and nap a lot, but their energy level skyrockets when they become teens (4 months to around a year). Energy level:
MEDIUM – Needs a daily 60-90 minute walk or window of quick paced exercise (minimum) in addition to potty break strolls (10-30 min each). Also needs significant socializing opportunities outside the home and mental stimulation at home like tricks training practice, chew items, and puzzle toys. (This is regardless of dog size – many small breeds were designed for lots of activity and will exhibit unwanted behavior when they’re understimulated.) 

Okay in the City:
Must have a home in the burbs! This girl can not do the city - can't even handle the nice calm parts of BK. 

Potty Training:
Yes! She's potty trained. Needs a few days to adjust but she gets it! 

Comfort With Strangers:
Shy with new people. Takes some time to adjust. 

Behavior w/Children:
Would be okay with older children - 12 years and up.

Social Behavior w/Other Dogs:
Awesome with other dogs!! 

Respectful Behavior w/ Other Animals (cats, small pets, etc.):
Would need to cat test her 

Mouthy Behavior:
Has shown a willingness to chew on paper, paper towels and small items on the floor. But she is never aggressive regarding it if you take it away from her. More or less seems to be a stealth stimulation characteristic. But is absolutely not mouthy when it comes to people, hands, feet, furniture. 

Separation Anxiety:
Adjusting. Does fairly well with separation.Might cry for a few minutes. Not consitent, seems more of a transition thing. 

Leash Manners:
Getting used to it. 

Cuddle Bug Level:
Loves a cuddle but also loves her space 

Jumping On People To Say Hello:
Calm Greetings. She is not a jumper. 

Crate Training:
Working on it. Has all of her meals in a crate. Goes in there for fun. We don't keep her in a crate for extended periods of time. 

Medical status:
Healthy as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP and Bordetella vaccines, spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. (For dogs under 4 months old, adopters will need to finish the DHPP vaccine series and administer the Rabies vaccine at 16 weeks of age.)

How did this dog end up with Social Tees?
Most of our dogs come via partner groups who help us save them from shelters where they are at risk of euthanasia in Tennessee, Los Angeles, and Puerto Rico. There are very few spay/neuter resources there and many more animals in those areas than there are people to adopt them. Rescue groups like ours bring them to the northeast where the desire for pets like these allows us to save their lives. 

PLEASE NOTE: We cannot guarantee any breed mix, exact age, or full grown size (if the dog is under a year old). We do our best with very educated guesses. 

This animal is not at the Social Tees office, all are in foster homes.
